title: Substack article, validation loss versus accuracy

The topic: why validation accuracy can keep improving while validation loss gets worse during training, what that pattern tells you about the model, and what to do about it. Include one small worked example with made-up numbers (a handful of examples with their predicted probabilities before and after a few more epochs) that shows the effect. Finish with one practical takeaway. No code, no bullet points, no headings inside the body.

content:
The Arrogant Student: When Your Model Wins the Battle but Loses the War

You have spent hours, perhaps days, training your model. You are watching the progress curves on your screen, and suddenly, you notice something deeply unsettling. Your validation accuracy, the metric you care about most, is climbing steadily. You are getting more predictions right. But simultaneously, your validation loss—the measure of how much error the model is making—is starting to climb too. It feels like a paradox. How can the model be getting more things right while simultaneously getting "worse"?

To understand this, you have to understand the difference between a judge and a scorekeeper. Accuracy is a scorekeeper. It only cares about a binary outcome: did you get the answer right or wrong? It doesn't care if you were 51% sure or 99% sure; it only cares that you crossed the threshold of being correct. Loss, however, is a judge of character. Loss cares about your confidence. It penalizes you not just for being wrong, but for being confidently wrong.

This divergence usually happens because your model is becoming an arrogant student. As training progresses, the model starts to move beyond learning the actual patterns in your data and begins to memorize the specific quirks and noise of the training set. This makes the model extremely "certain" about its predictions.

Imagine you are testing a student on ten questions. In the first round, the student gets seven questions right. When they get them right, they are only slightly sure, around 60% confident. When they get a question wrong, they are also somewhat unsure, perhaps 40% confident. Their accuracy is 70%, and their error (loss) is relatively low because they weren't very wrong when they failed.

In the second round, the student improves. They now get eight questions right, which looks like a massive victory. Their accuracy has jumped from 70% to 80%. However, they have also become incredibly stubborn. For the eight they got right, they are now 99% confident. But for the two they got wrong, they are now 99% certain of the wrong answer. Even though the student is "smarter" according to the accuracy score, the massive penalty for being so confidently wrong about those two questions causes their total error score to skyrocket. The model has become overconfident in its mistakes.

When you see this pattern, it is a clear signal of overfitting. Your model is not actually learning the underlying logic of the world; it is learning to be loud and certain about its guesses. It is finding ways to "win" the accuracy game by being slightly more right on some items, but in doing so, it is becoming dangerously certain about its errors on others. This is a sign that your model is losing its ability to generalize to new, unseen data.

To fix this, you need to reign in the model's ego. You can do this through a technique called regularization, which essentially adds a "complexity penalty" to the model, preventing it from becoming too extreme in its certainty. You can also use a technique called early stopping, which means you stop training the moment the loss starts to climb, even if the accuracy is still rising. Another option is label smoothing, which tells the model it shouldn't ever be 100% sure of anything, forcing it to remain a bit more humble in its predictions.

The practical takeaway is this: Never trust accuracy alone. If you want to know if your model is truly learning or just becoming a confident liar, always keep a close eye on your loss curve.
